prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which established the basis for incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six openings place GLP-1 first, and I agree on the merits rather than because of the tally. It is a complete arc from hormone physiology (proglucagon processing, the active GLP-1(7-36) amide, insulinotropic, glucagonostatic and satiety actions) through receptor and islet mechanism to therapies with large, sustained effects on glycaemia and body weight and, in outcome trials, cardiovascular and renal benefit. The mechanism is independently confirmed over two decades, the discovery is specific rather than a general platform, and the clinical and societal reach is exceptional. A basic-physiology prize to Holst, Drucker and Mojsov fits the committee's tradition of recognising discoveries about how the body works that then change medicine, and recognition now is timely.
statement.case_against: The credit is the real weakness. A three-person cap forces a choice between physiology and drug development, and leaving out Lotte Bjerre Knudsen, whose acylated long-acting analogues made the drugs, risks a citation that honours the science while skipping the step that delivered patient benefit. Mojsov's priority for identifying and synthesising the active peptide is contested, and I have not independently verified the history. If the committee decides the priority record is too unclear, the fallback is a narrower physiology citation or a Holst-Drucker-Knudsen configuration, and that would be a substantive change rather than a detail.

responses.point: Perlmann ranks optogenetics (B012) second as a general method that changed how circuits and physiology are tested, with Nagel, Hegemann and Deisseroth as the core.
responses.response: I agree on scientific merit; as a circuit neuroscientist I see the method in everyday use, and I ranked it second myself. I am cautious about the credit, though. Six credited names with a three-person cap leaves out Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenboeck, and Boyden's and Deisseroth's joint demonstration in neurons is arguably as decisive as channelrhodopsin characterisation. A trio of Nagel, Hegemann and Deisseroth is defensible but not clean. I would keep B012 as the strongest alternative, not combine it with B001, because a two-part prize would shrink the GLP-1 credit below what Drucker, Holst and Mojsov each need.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius places TNF blockade (B010) second as a clean two-person bench-to-bedside story with Feldmann and Maini, fully mature and arguably overdue.
responses.response: The credit is cleaner than for most candidates, and the case that recognition is overdue is fair. My reservation is conceptual. The discovery that TNF drives synovial cytokine networks is important, but the prize-level novelty is partly the principle of targeted cytokine blockade, which overlaps with IL-6 (B002) and later biologics, and the antibody engineering and cloning that made the drugs sit outside the credited names. I rank it below B001 and B017 for that reason, though I would not oppose it as a second part if the committee wants an immunology achievement alongside GLP-1.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks GLP-1 first but calls Mojsov's contribution decisive yet contested, and ranks the unfolded protein response (B051) second as conceptually original ER-to-nucleus signalling.
responses.response: I share the concern about Mojsov and it is the main thing I want to settle in discussion; I would not drop her without checking the priority record on the synthesised active peptide and its insulinotropic activity. On B051 I agree that Walter and Mori form a clean pair and the mechanism is conceptually elegant. The gap I see is clinical and physiological. Translation is early, and the PERK and ATF6 arms credited to others complicate the story. It stays below the top three for me, but it is a strong basic-science alternative to a cell-therapy prize.

responses.point: The chair ranks imatinib and BCR-ABL inhibition (B004) third, as the paradigm of targeted cancer therapy with Lydon, Druker and Sawyers as a coherent trio.
responses.response: The impact is beyond question and the maturity is complete. My hesitation is that the credit covers the therapeutic step only. The BCR-ABL and Philadelphia chromosome work by Rowley, Nowell, Baltimore and others lies outside the credited names, so a prize here would honour drug development and leave the discovery that made the target. Lasker-style recognition has already covered much of this ground. I put B017 ahead of it for novelty as a new modality, but I accept this is a close call and a legitimate difference.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers a physiology-centred citation (Holst, Drucker, Mojsov) or one that includes drug development (Knudsen), and which of the four to omit under the three-person cap.
Validity of Mojsov's priority claim for identifying and synthesising the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide; I have not independently verified the detailed history.
For optogenetics (B012), which three of six names best represent the discovery; I do not have a settled view on balancing channelrhodopsin discovery against neuronal deployment.
Whether a two-part prize pairing GLP-1 with a second achievement would dilute the credit more than it adds.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. I work on motor circuits in zebrafish and lamprey, and optogenetics (B012) is a tool for that field, so I treat my interest as expertise and not an institutional tie. I co-authored with Thomas Perlmann (2009, dopamine neurons from stem cells) and with Sten Grillner and Patrik Ernfors, none of whom is a credited candidate.
